senses: The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction.
Sexual procreation between a man and a woman or transfer of the sperm from male to female; usually applied to the mating process in nonhuman animals; coitus; coition.
ety: From Middle French copulation, from Latin copulo (“to join, unite, connect”).
examples: Solomon, who was one of the Deity's favorities, had a copulation cabinet composed of seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.

senses: A net or dragnet used for trawling.
A long fishing line having many short lines bearing hooks attached to it; a setline.
An exhaustive search.
ety: 16th century, borrowed from Dutch tragelen (“to pull with a towline, trawl”), from Middle Dutch traghelen, from traghel (“dragnet”) (presumably from Latin tragula (“dragnet”)), and as such root-cognate with English drag and dray.
examples: I embarked on a trawl through my uncle's papers in search of his missing will.

senses: A round sweet and juicy stone fruit, resembling peach or plum in taste, with a yellow-orange flesh, lightly fuzzy skin and a large seed inside.
The apricot tree, Prunus armeniaca.
A pale yellow-orange colour, like that of an apricot fruit.
A dog with an orange-coloured coat.
The junction of the brain and brain stem on a target, used as an aiming point to ensure a one-shot kill.
ety: Alteration of apricock (with influence from French abricot), itself an alteration of abrecock (with influence from Latin apricum (“sunny place”)), from dialectal Catalan abrecoc, abricoc, variants of standard albercoc, from Arabic الْبَرْقُوق (al-barqūq, “plums”), from Byzantine Greek βερικοκκία (berikokkía, “apricot tree”), from Ancient Greek πραικόκιον (praikókion), from Late Latin (persica) praecocia (literally “(peaches) which ripen early”), (mālum) praecoquum (literally “(apple) which ripens early”). Doublet of precocious.
examples: I'd aim right for the apricot. The medulla. You'd die instantly.

senses: A style of music featuring words chanted over house music, originating in Johannesburg during the 1990s.
The meme or milieu associated with the music style.
ety: From Camtho, from Afrikaans kwaai (“cool”, literally “angry”).
examples: The residue of this otherworldliness is still audible in contemporary kwaito, which consistently thwarts any simple identification with ethnicity, language, or social position.
Sivuyile is part of the kwaito generation.

senses: Gruel or thin porridge.
A Scottish form of cottage cheese.
ety: Alteration of Early Scots crud (“curd”), cognate with Early Modern English and Middle English crud, crudde (14th c.), crodde, of unknown origin.
examples: The old woman shuffled out from the back room with a handful of coal and a bowl of crowdie for the boy.

senses: An excessive masculine pride, exaggerated masculinity.
Male chauvinism, misogyny.
ety: First attested 1940, from American Spanish machismo, from Spanish macho (“male”), + suffix -ismo (“-ism”).
examples: The tragedy of machismo is that a man is never quite man enough.

With machismo, Christian nationalism and callousness toward the lives of US troops, they say, Hegseth’s puerile displays on TV are aimed at sating Trump’s desire for a warmonger worthy of the manosphere.

senses: Leptoptilos crumeniferus, a large wading bird native to Africa, with a naked head and neck adapted for scavenging.
A person having five-eighths black ancestry; the offspring of a mulatto and a griffe.
A kind of thrown raw silk, naturally nearly white, but capable of being dyed without scouring.
A thin fabric made from this silk, as for scarves.
ety: From French marabou, an older spelling of marabout.
examples: Madimarian , a Marabou, killed me a bullock; I give him one bottle of powder.

senses: Thin, unleavened bread in Jewish cuisine.
A piece of the above bread.
ety: When stressed on the first syllable, from Yiddish מצה (matse), from Hebrew מַצָּה (matsá); pronunciations stressed on the second syllable are borrowed directly from Hebrew.
examples: Matzo is eaten by Jews on Passover.
Like the Kopelmans, they have a Christmas tree with dreidel ornaments and a menorah, which they light each night. Pham learned to cook matzo ball soup.

senses: Any of several different plants, from several genera, having bluish flowers.
Several plant genera in the family Rubiaceae, notably Houstonia and Oldenlandiopsis.
A kind of blue woolen cloth.
ety: From Middle English blawede, blewed, blewet, bloued, blowed, bloweth, from Middle English blewe (“blue”). Alternatively, perhaps from Old French bleuet (diminutive of bleu (“blue”)). Compare modern French bleuet (“cornflower”). By surface analysis, blue + -et.
examples: My breathing shakes the bluet like a breeze ….
They passed undulating fields of wheat speckled with the confetti of poppies and bluets.

senses: A circumstance in which a choice must be made between three options that seem equally undesirable.
A situation in which a choice must be made among three desirable options, only two of which are possible at the same time.
ety: The word is modelled on dilemma, with di- (“two, twice, double”) replaced by tri- (“three”), equivalent to tri- + lemma.
examples: With all these dilemmas and trilemmas crowding the mind, if one did not know better, one might be tempted to doubt whether any such versions were ever made at all.

senses: Any tangible object or thing, especially one that is short and thick.
A nonsense word or placeholder, often used incongruously in self-deprecating or doomer-like speech.
Something that is correct, agreeable to consensus, or without fault, as part of a straw man.
ety: From chunk. Compare humongous (“extremely large”, adjective) or dingus (“any object or thing; a foolish person”, noun), and chonk. James Stephanie Sterling was credited with coining the term “chungus” in 2012, though it did not see wide usage until around 2018 with the rise of the “Big Chungus” meme. The Big Chungus meme is derived from the Looney Tunes episode Wabbit Twouble.
examples: He’s a big chungus / He’s a big chunky boy / Such a big bun, yes / We are so overjoyed
Meanwhile, memes about "Chungus" have been circulating on their own subreddit for over a year, and "Big Chungus" since Fall 2018.
Close to a hundred Magnite and 30 Hollomite in these two chunguses

senses: Enough to fill a skin.
Enough alcoholic drink to cause inebriation.
ety: From skin + -ful.
examples: I wasn't thinking straight – I'd had a skinful that night.
When methodist preachers come down, A-preaching that drinking is sinful, I'll wager the rascals a crown, They always preach best with a skinful.

senses: An ancient religious stone artifact, or baetylus, used to denote the direction of the "center" of the world.

The theological proposition that the world was created with certain indicia of a history which had not actually occurred (such as the humans who had never been connected to umbilical cords being created with navels).
A raised central point; a boss.
The center or hub.
ety: From Ancient Greek ὀμφαλός (omphalós, “navel”). Doublet of navel.
examples: Here I was, embosomed in the very nave, the very omphalos of furtive femininity—a prize patron of the women's restaurant, a member, privy to its innermost secrets.
The place in which this statue stood, Malalas writes, was called “the omphalos of the city.”

senses: Running; flowing.
Having successive letters joined together.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French cursif, from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.
examples: Then Mambro handed me his manuscript, a sheaf of loose pages really, his cursive handwriting scrawled over them, the exaggerated tails of the f’s and the j’s, the distinct loop of the q.

senses: The burning of moxa against the skin to treat pain or illness.
ety: Blend of moxa (“mugwort”) + combustion, literally “burning of mugwort”, with the connecting -i- usual in Latinate vocabulary.
examples: Traditional Chinese medicine includes herbal remedy, diet therapy, use of animal secretion and organs, acupuncture, massage, moxibustion (the application of a burning moxa plant to skin), and other folk methods.

senses: A small two-wheeled cart; (historical) a chariot.
A period of intense work, especially group work undertaken to meet a deadline.
ety: Borrowed from French charrette (literally “small cart”). In the modern sense popularized by the US design supply chain Charrette (1969–2009).
examples: He was in fierce wrath, because Patrasche had been a strong and much-enduring animal, and because he himself had now the hard task of pushing his charette all the way to Louvain.
A shaggy Indian pony came ambling around the corner between the long shafts of a charette.

senses: To cut in or into with a sharp instrument; to carve; to engrave.
ety: From Middle French inciser.
examples: The executioner’s blade is incised with Christ’s crown of thorns, and with the words of a prayer.

senses: Of the nettle plant and similar physical causes, to sting, causing a rash in someone.
To pique, irritate, vex or provoke.
ety: From Middle English netle, netel, from Old English netle, netele, netel, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā (cognate with Old Saxon netila, Middle Dutch netele (modern Dutch netel), German Nessel, Middle Danish nædlæ (“nettle”)), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *natǭ (of unknown origin, perhaps from the same source as net).
examples: The children were badly nettled after playing in the field.

senses: A person who studies or practices ornithology.
ety: From ornithology + -ist.
examples: Mr. Worple in his spare time was what is known as an ornithologist. He had written a book called American Birds, and was writing another, to be called More American Birds.

senses: A bid in which the bidder asserts that he or she will not take any tricks.
One who has their genitals (and sometimes nipples) surgically removed (nullification) as a form of body modification.
ety: From null + -o.
examples: It takes a better nullo hand to raise nullos than to bid them. Dummy shows. A player who has once been called off from nullos by his partner should never return to them.

senses: To fill with great delight or joy; to fascinate or captivate.
ety: From en- + rapture.
examples: Her song enraptured the audience with vivid images of the Scandinavian landscapes.

senses: Deviation from moral normality; extreme wickedness, nefariousness, or cruelty.
A breach of law or morality; a transgression, an act of evil or wickedness.
ety: From Late Middle English ēnorme (“monstrous or unnatural act; enormity”), from Old French énormité (“enormity”), from Latin ēnormitās (“irregularity; enormity”), from ēnōrmis (“irregular, unusual; enormous, immense”) + -itās (suffix forming nouns indicating states of being). Ēnōrmis is derived from e- (a variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘out; away’) + nōrma (“norm, standard”) + -is (Latin suffix forming adjectives from nouns).
examples: Not until the war ended and journalists were able to enter Cambodia did the world really become aware of the enormity of Pol Pot’s oppression.
I had an obscure feeling that all was not over, and that he would still commit some signal crime, which by its enormity should almost efface the recollection of the past.
In 1650 Lieutenant William Jackson was in trouble for holding, among many other enormities, ‘community of all things’, including, apparently, wives.

senses: A shrub (Aspalathus linearis) from which a tisane (herbal tea) is made.
The tisane (herbal tea) made from this plant.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Afrikaans rooibos (literally “redbush”), from Dutch rooi (“red”) + bos (“bush”). Compare related honeybush via Afrikaans heuningbos from heuning (“honey”) + bos (“bush”).
examples: The air is aromatic with buchu (Rutaceae), pines, rooibos (Aspalathus linearis), and, of course, the cedars for which these mountains are named.
Love it or hate it, rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) is as much a part of this region as rock art, velskoen and stunning spring flowers.
During the past twenty years or so farmers in the Cedarberg region, from Citrusdal to Nieuwoudtville, have raised the rooibos tea industry from obscurity to minor boom.

senses: To convert or be converted into clinker.
ety: From Dutch klinkaerd, later klinker, from klinken (“to ring, resound”).
examples: This burning has baked and clinkered the adjacent strata, producing a very resistant formation, which rises with conspicuous abruptness from the flat terrace underlain by the soft Lebo shale member.

senses: To make moral reflections (on, upon, about or over something); to regard acts and events as involving a moral.
To say (something) expressing a moral reflection or judgment.
To render moral; to correct the morals of; to give the appearance of morality to.
To give a moral quality to; to affect the moral quality of, either for better or worse.
ety: From Old French moraliser, equivalent to moral + -ize.
examples: One hoped, and the other despaired: they chose their own lots, and were righteously doomed to endure them. But you’ll not want to hear my moralising, Mr. Lockwood; you’ll judge, as well as I can, all these things:
The usual conduct of the spoilt child! Had she not witnessed it, and moralized upon it, in other families?
A Cake Related Fatphobic Incident — or CRFI for short — is that moment when it's time to eat delicious cake, and an otherwise joyous experience gets ruined by a moralizing impulse.

senses: Exhibiting dissonance; not agreeing; not harmonizing or melodizing.
Exhibiting dissonance; not agreeing or harmonizing.
ety: From Middle French dissonant.
examples: The music was filled with dissonant chords.

senses: A wax secreted by bees from which they make honeycomb; or, the processed form of this wax used in the manufacture of various goods.
ety: From bee + -s- + wax.
examples: The candle was made entirely of natural beeswax.
She polished the furniture with beeswax to give it a shine.
The beekeeper collected honey and beeswax from the hives.

senses: A ritual bath in which various Jewish purifications are performed.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew מִקְוֶה (mikvé, “collection [of water]”).
examples: On the night before her wedding Channa Washinsky would certainly have immersed herself in the ritually cleansing waters of the mikveh.

senses: Having the form of an orb; round; spherical.
ety: From orb + -ed.
examples: Orbed is the moon and bright, And the stars they glisten, glisten,

senses: Like a prig.
ety: From prig + -ish.
examples: To ride; to dance; she had adored all that. Or going long walks in the country, talking, about books, what to do with one’s life, for young people were amazingly priggish—oh, the things one had said!

senses: The use of a word or phrase to replace another one that is more offensive, blunt or vulgar.
A word or phrase that replaces another in this way.
ety: Recorded since 1656; from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός (euphēmismós), from εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō), from εὔφημος (eúphēmos, “uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φημί (phēmí, “to speak, say”).
examples: When it is said of the martyr St. Stephen, that “he fell asleep,” instead of—he died, the euphemism partakes of the nature of metaphor, intimating a resemblance between sleep and the death of such a person.

Euphemistic language turns up in many areas of American life in a variety of situations. Not all euphemisms are alike, but they have one thing in common: They obscure meaning rather than enhance it; they shade the truth.

senses: Including or given to slang.
Loud in dress, manner, and conversation; flashy, vulgar.
ety: From slang + -y.
examples: His slangy speech was almost uncomprehensible to anyone over the age of 18.

senses: Injured, or not functioning properly (with respect to legs).
ety: Origin obscure and uncertain. Possibly from the English dialectal (North Midlands) adjective game (“lame”), Welsh cam (“crooked”), or from Irish cam (“bent”), by way of Shelta. Compare also Old Occitan gambi (“lame, limping”), related to Old Occitan gamba (“leg”) (see also French jambe (“leg”), English gam (“leg”)).
examples: I have got a gammy leg, and can't walk far.
However, I had been doing a lot of walking and my gammy leg began to give me trouble.
I'm not exactly spectacular at the moment with a gammy knee that sometimes lets me down and hair that looks as if it's been cut with a knife and fork.

senses: Afflicted with a squint.
Sidelong, slanting, askew.
ety: From squint + -y.
examples: That frame is a bit squinty, you'll have to right it.

senses: Causing obstructions.
ety: From obstruct + -ive.
examples: I wanted to see his report on me, but my manager was being obstructive.

senses: Exhibiting sameness, without variety; monotonous.
ety: From same + -y.
examples: Nowadays, its apartments go to finance workers who work nearby, while its bars are samey places encircled by moats of urine.
This was a bubble, a mass delusion among operators convinced that Britain’s appetite for samey chain restaurants was insatiable.
Of course, there are only so many formerly blind people you can watch being given the gift of sight before it starts getting a little samey.

senses: A month of an average of approximately 29.53 days, measured from a lunar phase until the return of that same phase.
The irregular period from one new moon until the next.
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lūnātiō.
examples: And there is not the moon seen in all the lunation, save only the second quarter.

senses: A vulgar individual, especially one who emphasizes or is oblivious to his or her vulgar qualities.
ety: From vulgar + -ian. Compare Late Latin vulgārius, Latin vulgāris.
examples: He was by this time on the deck, but he had the art to be quite unapproachable; the friendliest vulgarian, three parts drunk, would have known better than take liberties...
She is a bitch in heat, a mindless grinning vulgarian, and a shrewd and desperate schemer all at once.
Leading the attack on the president's very citizenship is the professional vulgarian Donald Trump, who gets away with the kind of preposterous, race-based comments granted few black public figures.

senses: To settle (a place) with colonists, and hence make (a place) into a colony.
To settle among and establish control over (the indigenous people of an area).
To begin a colony or colonies.
To intrude into and take over (the autonomy, experience, social movement, etc, of a less powerful person or group); to commandeer or appropriate.
ety: From colony + -ize.
examples: When you are colonized by dangerous bacteria their presence in your body does no damage. You become a reservoir for those little stinkers.
The administration finally sent a naval vessel to return the 368 survivors to the United States in 1864. This ended official efforts to colonize blacks.
What disservice would be done if issues regarding sexualities in organisations were side-lined by a heteronormative impetus to colonise queer theory?

senses: Decorated with sequins.
ety: From sequin + -ed.
examples: She wore a blue sequined dress.
She was naked except for a brief vee of black lace and a black sequined star in the centre of each breast and the thin black domino across her eyes.
Was always kinda partial to Roy Rogers actually. I really like those sequined shirts.
